title: Ansoff Matrix Deep Dive
welcome_lead: Four growth routes - pick the one that matches your risk appetite.
meta_desc: A-Level Strategy: Ansoff matrix with risk profile.
final_note: Risk rises the further you move from familiar products and markets.

concepts.def: Existing products to existing markets - lowest risk.
Existing products to new markets - moderate risk.
New products to existing markets - moderate risk.
New products to new markets - highest risk.
Diversifying into linked industries with synergies.
Conglomerate move with no obvious synergies.

walkthroughs.body_html: Plot products (existing vs new) against markets (existing vs new). Each quadrant has a typical strategy - penetration drives loyalty schemes; product development drives R&D.
Penetration may grow share by 1 to 5 percent; diversification can double the firm or sink it. Expected returns rise with risk - but so does the chance of failure.
Coca-Cola's launch of Coke Zero is product development. Tesla entering Europe is market development. Amazon's move into film studios is diversification.

mcqs.q: What four growth strategies does Ansoff's Matrix identify?
options: Market penetration (existing product, existing market), market development (existing product, new market), product development (new product, existing market), diversification (new product, new market).
Porter's strategies are about marketing channels.
Ansoff's Matrix shows market share against profit.
Ansoff's Matrix is about analysing competitors.

mcqs.q: What are Porter's two main generic strategies for competitive advantage?
options: Porter's strategies are about marketing channels.
Porter's Five Forces are five physical security measures for a factory.
Porter says businesses should pursue both low cost and differentiation at once.
Cost leadership (being the lowest-cost producer) and differentiation (offering unique value customers will pay more for) — Porter argues firms should choose one or the other.

Competitive rivalry, threat of new entrants, threat of substitutes, bargaining power of suppliers, bargaining power of buyers — together determining industry attractiveness and potential profitability.
Porter's Five Forces are five business strategies a firm should choose between.
Porter's Five Forces are five physical security measures for a factory.
